wartsila.generated_disclosure:
### G1-2 – Management of relationships with suppliers

Suppliers play a significant role in Wärtsilä’s delivery process. Wärtsilä seeks close relationships with key suppliers to ensure a shared understanding of, and compliance with, process and product requirements. Open and continuous dialogue supports supplier performance, knowledge sharing and innovation, and enables strategic suppliers to integrate more closely into Wärtsilä’s value chain. Engagement methods include regular dialogue on supplier performance, the supplier portal eTool, supplier development support, Supplier Days, assessments and audits.

Wärtsilä has defined processes for supplier selection, compliance assessment and relationship development. General supplier requirements cover compliance with applicable legislation, environmental aspects, quality, occupational health and safety management, social performance and cyber security. Product- and service-specific requirements apply in addition to these general requirements. Suppliers must demonstrate compliance to obtain approved supplier status, and the requirements are incorporated into standard supply agreements.

Suppliers are assessed and managed through the Supplier Relationship Management tool, a risk-based assessment and management system. Before a relationship begins, potential suppliers are assessed with regard to their offering, risk level and compliance with Wärtsilä’s requirements. The basic risk assessment considers both supplier- and country-level risks and is also applied to existing suppliers through periodic reassessments. The Supply Management team reviews supplier submissions and determines whether further assessment is required. Low-risk suppliers may be approved based on the basic assessment, while medium- and high-risk suppliers are, as a default, subject to a detailed assessment. This assesses capabilities and capacity and provides additional information supporting the approval decision.

Supplier compliance is monitored through performance indicators, audits and continuous supplier performance management. Wärtsilä also uses an online solution for supply-chain risk identification, assessment and monitoring, with more than 2,000 suppliers followed against defined key criteria. Supplier and subcontractor risks are managed through supplier requirements, the supplier management system and business continuity planning, with responsibilities assigned to the businesses and Supply Management. Where requirements are not met, suppliers may be banned; corrective action can lead to an improved rating.

The supplier management system is assessed and upgraded regularly. The risk-based tool was introduced for new suppliers in 2018 and for existing suppliers in 2019, with development and deployment continuing thereafter.

For the 2022 reporting year, the average time to pay an invoice, measured from the date on which the contractual or statutory payment term began, was 74 days. The available metric is not disaggregated by supplier size. No 2022 supplier-rating coverage target or outcome is reported in the available data.

### E1-6 – Gross Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3 and total GHG emissions

ASML monitors greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with its own operations as part of its environmental-efficiency activities. Climate-related focus areas include product stewardship, the energy efficiency of products, renewable electricity and environmental efficiency in our own operations. Responsibility for these focus areas is associated with Products & Technology and Operations.

For 2019, gross Scope 2 GHG emissions were **141,400 tCO₂e**. This amount is reported on both a market-based and location-based basis and relates to ASML’s consolidated accounting group under a financial-control approach. The same amount is identified as relating to own operations. The available dataset also assigns 141,400 tCO₂e to both upstream and downstream value-chain fields for Scope 2. As these entries represent the same reported Scope 2 amount, they have not been added together in determining emissions.

| GHG emissions category | 2019 |
|---|---:|
| Gross Scope 1 emissions | Not available in the provided 2019 data |
| Gross Scope 2 emissions – location-based | 141,400 tCO₂e |
| Gross Scope 2 emissions – market-based | 141,400 tCO₂e |
| Gross Scope 3 emissions | Not available in the provided 2019 data |
| Other Scope 3 category | 0 tCO₂e |
| Total GHG emissions | Not determinable from the provided data |

ASML’s Scope 1 footprint has historically been defined as emissions from the combustion of natural gas and purchased CO₂. Scope 2 emissions have historically been calculated by multiplying electricity consumption at manufacturing locations by applicable local conversion factors. The evidence available for 2019 does not provide the underlying activity data, emission factors, treatment of renewable electricity instruments or separate Scope 1 emissions required to reconcile the 2019 result.

For context, ASML reported an own-operations CO₂ footprint of **32.9 ktonnes in 2018**, comprising **17.5 ktonnes of direct Scope 1 emissions** and **15.4 ktonnes of indirect Scope 2 emissions**. The available information does not establish that the 2018 and 2019 figures have consistent boundaries or methodologies; consequently, no year-on-year trend has been calculated.

A value of zero is reported only for the “other Scope 3” category. It does not demonstrate that total Scope 3 emissions were zero, as no complete Scope 3 inventory or category breakdown is available. Accordingly, gross total GHG emissions cannot be calculated without adding unsupported assumptions to the reported information.
